pll1d15c1-d1e3477.summary: Asks whether the Spirit, given by Father and Son, which is his temporal procession or mission, is also given by himself; if so, he is also sent and proceeds from himself.

pll1d15c1-d1e3480.summary: Answers that the Spirit is both God and Gift, so he gives and is given: as God he gives, as Gift he is given. Since giving the Spirit is a work of God, common and undivided to the three persons, he is given by himself as well as by Father and Son.
claims: The Spirit gives as God and is given as Gift.
Divine operations are common to the three persons.
The Spirit is given by himself.

pll1d15c1-d1e3485.summary: Cites De Trinitate XV: as 'body of flesh' is flesh, the 'gift of the Spirit' is the Spirit. He is God's gift insofar as given, but God in himself even if given to none, coeternal before he was given. Being given does not make him lesser, for he gives himself as God ('the Spirit blows where he wills'). Otherwise Father and Son could do what the Spirit cannot.
claims: The gift of the Spirit is the Spirit himself.
The Spirit is God even when given to no one.
Being given does not make the Spirit lesser.
The Spirit gives himself.

pll1d15c1-d1e3511.summary: Draws the consequence: if the Spirit did not give himself, Father and Son would do a work he does not. So he gives himself, and since temporal procession or mission is the giving, which is God's work, he proceeds temporally and is sent from himself.
claims: The Spirit proceeds temporally from himself and is sent by himself.
Mission is giving, and giving is a common divine work.

pll1d15c1-d1e3514.summary: Notes that this should not surprise, since Augustine in De Trinitate II says the Son also was sent not only by the Father but by himself and the Spirit, and asks how Son and Spirit can be sent when each is everywhere as God.
claims: The Son is sent by the Father, by himself, and by the Spirit.
How omnipresent persons can be sent is a question.

pll1d15c1-d1e3528.summary: Gathers the texts on sending: the Father will send the Spirit, the Son will send him, the Son came from the Father, God sent his Son, and yet God fills heaven and earth (Jer 23:24).
claims: Scripture says both Son and Spirit are sent.
God fills heaven and earth.

pll1d15c1-d1e3582.summary: Concludes that since God is everywhere, so are the Son and the Spirit, so they were sent where they already were.
claims: Son and Spirit are everywhere.
They were sent where they already were.

pl-l1d15c1.summary: Asks whether the Spirit, given by Father and Son (which is his temporal procession or mission), is also given by himself. Lombard answers yes: the Spirit is both God and Gift, so he gives as God and is given as Gift. Since giving is a common and undivided work of the three persons, he is given, sent, and proceeds temporally from himself as well. Augustine supports this ('the Spirit blows where he wills'), adding that otherwise Father and Son could do something the Spirit could not. Augustine also says the Son was sent by himself and the Spirit, which raises the question of how persons who are everywhere can be sent where they already were.
claims: The Holy Spirit gives as God and is given as Gift.
The giving of the Spirit is a common, undivided work of the three persons.
The Spirit gives himself, and so is sent and proceeds temporally from himself.
Otherwise the Father and Son could do what the Spirit cannot.
The Son is likewise sent by the Father, by himself, and by the Spirit.
Since Son and Spirit are everywhere, they are sent where they already were.
